# The Simulator {#sec-simulator}

This appendix documents `sim.collection`, the function that makes the book's simulated tree-ring data. [Chapter 2](02AdditiveModel.qmd) explains the basic model behind it. [Chapter 3](03SimulatedCollection.qmd) builds the simulated data used in the rest of the book. This appendix covers the details including what the arguments do as well as the output. When a chapter says "the simulated collection," it means the one made with `seed = 1`.

The function lives in the book's `R/` folder and isn't part of `dplR`. Every chapter loads it the same way.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(dplR)
source("R/sim-collection.R")
sim <- sim.collection(seed = 1)
names(sim)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "rwl"   "ids"   "truth"
```


:::
:::




It returns three things. `sim$rwl` is the collection as you would have it after measuring, an `rwl` object with the years as row names and any dating errors left in. `sim$ids` says which tree and which core each series is, in the form that functions like `rwi.stats` and `treeMean` want. `sim$truth` is what you never get from trees you cored. It holds each part of every ring separately, and a record of what was planted where. @sec-sim-returns lists it field by field.

## The Collection



The default collection is 20 trees with two cores each, all cored in 2025. Two cores from each of twenty trees is the design the Cook Book recommends for a ring-width chronology [@CookBook, p. 27]. Tree 1 is the oldest, with its pith in 1646, and tree 20 is the youngest, with its pith in 1906. The ages are spaced on a square, so old trees are few and the sample depth thins going back in time, as it does in most collections. Each core misses the pith by a few rings, a Poisson draw with a mean of five, so the two cores from one tree start in different years. [The Simulated Collection](03SimulatedCollection.qmd) shows the collection as a segment plot.

By default every tree is alive when it is cored. `dead` adds dead trees, the snags and remnant wood a collection can mix with living ones. `dead = list(frac = 0.3, span = 300)` kills 30% of the trees, each in a year drawn uniformly from the 300 years before `end.year`. A dead tree keeps its age, so its pith moves back with its outer ring and the collection reaches further back in time. The series then end in different years. The release tree and any tree with a planted dating error stay alive, because their years are given for a tree cored in `end.year`. `sim$truth$pith` gives each tree's outer ring beside its pith.

The series are named for the site, a two-digit tree number and a core letter, so SIM03A is the first core from tree 3, and `autoread.ids` reads the names the same way `sim$ids` does.

One thing to watch. The tables in `sim$truth` start in 1646, the year of the oldest pith, while `sim$rwl` starts in 1650, the first ring anyone measured. So the truth tables begin with four rows that have no rings in them. Some functions return `NaN` for rows like that (`pointer`, for example), so drop them first.

## How a Ring Is Built

The parts follow Cook's aggregate model [@Cook1990model], which [chapter 2](02AdditiveModel.qmd) lays out. They are added on the log scale and exponentiated, so the spread of the widths grows with their level the way it does in wood. One ring in core $j$ of tree $i$ is

$$\log R_{ijt} = \log A_{it} + M_{ijt} + \delta D1_{it} + \delta D2_{it}, \qquad M_{ijt} = \phi M_{ij,t-1} + C_t + T_{it} + E_{ijt}$$

and the measured width is $R_{ijt}$ rounded to `digits = 2`, or 0.01 mm. If a ring rounds to zero the function warns you, because `dplR` reads a zero as an absent ring. The rest of this section takes the parts one at a time.

### Age and Size, $A_{it}$

Each tree adds about the same basal area every year, `bai = 600` mm² in a typical tree. Trees differ in how fast they grow. Each tree's rate is drawn from a lognormal distribution with a log standard deviation of `bai.sdlog = 0.4`, independently of its age. A young tree ramps up to its rate over its first few decades, and `juv = 25` sets how quickly. The ring width is the change in radius that a year's area adds, so the rings thin as the stem grows. That is Cook's geometric argument for $A_t$ in an open stand.

With those defaults every open-grown tree has the same shape of age trend, scaled by its growth rate. `bai.trend` lets each tree's basal area increment change with age instead. A tree's yearly area is multiplied by $e^{\beta_i \cdot \text{age}/100}$, with $\beta_i$ drawn for each tree from a normal distribution with a mean of zero and a standard deviation of `bai.trend`. A tree with a negative $\beta_i$ adds less area as it ages, so its rings thin faster than geometry alone would make them. A tree with a positive $\beta_i$ keeps adding more, so its rings level off or even widen late in life. At `bai.trend = 0.3` the shapes spread out enough that one regional curve fits them poorly. On the true $A$ of the open-grown collection at seed 1, the median core's standard deviation from the regional curve on the log scale went from 0.011 to 0.073. A negative exponential fit to each core still followed its own tree closely, with a median misfit of 0.010. Each tree's $\beta_i$ comes back in `sim$truth$growth`, beside its growth rate. The default, `bai.trend = 0`, keeps the one shape.

By default a tree's growth rate has nothing to do with its age. `bai.age` ties them together. It is the correlation between the log of a tree's growth rate and its age, from −1 to 1. A negative value makes the old trees slow growers and the young ones fast, which is what Briffa and Melvin expect in a collection of living trees, since a tree that grows slowly takes longer to reach the size where trees die [@BriffaMelvin2011, p. 122-123]. The spread of growth rates stays at `bai.sdlog`. Over 50 collections with no release, event or dating errors, a regional curve made a chronology that drifted away from the true one by about −0.01 index units per century at `bai.age = 0`, +0.05 at −0.3 and +0.10 at −0.6, measured where at least 10 cores overlap. The default, `bai.age = 0`, keeps rate and age independent.

In a closed canopy, Cook argued, $A_t$ has no predictable shape at all [@Cook1990model, p. 100]. So half the trees (`compete.frac = 0.5`) get a competition history on top of the geometry. It is a slow random wander, an AR(1) series with a coefficient of `compete.phi = 0.97`, smoothed with an 11-year running mean so it changes over decades, and scaled to a standard deviation of `compete = 0.3` on the log scale. Both cores of a tree share it. It counts as part of the age trend, so `sim$truth$age` includes it, and `sim$truth$competition` lists the crowded trees. Set `compete = 0` for open-grown trees only.

### Climate, $C_t$

There is one climate series affecting every tree. By default it is random numbers with a little memory so that each year keeps `climate.phi = 0.3` of the year before, on top of its own new shock. You can hand the function a climate series instead, through `climate`, as a numeric vector named by year that covers every year from the oldest pith to `end.year`. The function rescales it to the size it needs and keeps its shape, and it ignores `climate.phi`. [Detrending](09Detrending.qmd) does this to give the site slow swings in climate. `sim$truth$climate` is the series as it went into the trees, on the log scale and before the trees' memory.

By default every tree feels the climate with the same strength, as in Cook's model. `sens.sdlog` gives each tree its own sensitivity instead, a multiplier on the climate drawn from a lognormal distribution and scaled so that its mean square is 1. Sensitive trees swing more and follow the climate more closely, and complacent ones swing less. Trees that differ in sensitivity also agree with each other less, so the between-tree correlation falls under `rbar.bt`. On the true fast part, averaged over 200 collections, it went from about 0.50 with `sens.sdlog = 0` to 0.44 at 0.3 and 0.32 at 0.6. Each tree's multiplier comes back in `sim$truth$sensitivity`.

### Noise, $T_{it}$ and $E_{ijt}$

Cook's $E_t$ is everything left over. The simulation splits it in two. $T_{it}$ belongs to a tree, so both of its cores carry it. $E_{ijt}$ belongs to a single core. The split is what makes two cores from one tree agree more than two trees do. Neither comes back on its own in `sim$truth`. Both are inside `memory.noise`.

### Memory, $\phi$

Climate and both kinds of noise go through an AR(1) filter that carries `phi = 0.5` of last year's value into this year. It stands in for the needles, roots and stored sugar that a good year leaves for the next one. Cook's first version of the model puts the persistence the trees share into $C_t$ [@cook1985, p. 23] and keeps $E_t$ free of memory. Filtering the noise as well is the simulation's addition, so a tree's own good and bad runs carry over along with the ones all the trees share. The filter runs for 50 years before each tree's first ring, so the memory is already up to strength when the tree starts. `sim$truth$memory.noise` holds $M_{ijt}$, the filtered sum, on the log scale.

### Disturbance, $D1_{it}$ and $D2_{it}$

Both disturbances are a pulse, a jump of `size` on the log scale in one year, which then decays exponentially and falls by a factor of $e$ every `decay` years. `release` is $D1_{it}$ in one tree. By default tree 10 doubles its growth in 1950 (`size = log(2)`), and the boost fades over decades (`decay = 25`). `event` is $D2_{it}$. By default, in 1880, half the trees standing at the time (`frac = 0.5`) have their growth halved (`size = -log(2)`), and they recover over a decade or so (`decay = 8`). Which trees it hits is drawn at random, and `sim$truth$event$trees` lists them by number.

Cook defines $D2_t$ by its turning up in every tree [@Cook1990model, p. 102]. His dissertation puts it in "virtually all affected trees" [@cook1985, p. 32], which leaves room for an event that misses some. It has an $i$ here because it hits about half the trees. Hitting half the trees keeps the event visible as something other than climate, and knowing which trees were hit is how [Detrending](09Detrending.qmd) shows what a curve does to an event. `frac = 1` gives Cook's version.

The disturbances are added after the memory filter, so each one keeps its shape. Cook treats disturbance as a shock that passes through a tree's memory the way climate does [@CookBook, p. 130], and the simulation doesn't. `sim$truth$disturbance` holds $D1_{it} + D2_{it}$ for each core, on the log scale.

### Dating Errors

Errors go in last, and only into `sim$rwl`. `sim$truth$rwl` keeps the widths as the trees grew them. `errors` is a data frame with three columns: the series, the true calendar year of the ring, and the type. A `"missing"` ring is deleted, and every ring inside it is labeled a year too late. A `"false"` ring splits one ring into two, at 40% and 60% of its width, and every ring inside it is labeled a year too early. A series can take more than one error. The default deletes the 1800 ring from SIM03A.

## Setting How Well the Trees Agree {#sec-sim-agree}

You don't set the size of each part directly. You set how well the cores agree, and the function works out the sizes. Three arguments do it.

- `sd.hf = 0.25` is the standard deviation of $M_{ijt}$ on the log scale, the year-to-year part of growth.
- `rbar.bt = 0.4` is the share of that variance that comes from climate. It is the correlation you would expect between two trees.
- `rbar.wt = 0.6` is the share that comes from climate and tree noise together. It is the correlation you would expect between two cores of one tree.

Core noise gets the rest. When the climate has memory, all three parts are shrunk by one common factor, so $M_{ijt}$ keeps the standard deviation you asked for and the shares stay where you set them.

The targets apply to the year-to-year part with the memory taken out. So they are what you would expect from prewhitened indices if detrending were perfect. The truth lets you try that. `exp(sim$truth$memory.noise)` is each core with its age trend and its disturbances divided out exactly.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Each core with its age trend and disturbances removed exactly, labeled as
# indices so that rwi.stats accepts it
perfect <- as.rwi(exp(sim$truth$memory.noise))

# rbar with rwi.stats' default, Spearman's rank correlation, and then with
# Pearson's
spearmanStats <- rwi.stats(perfect, sim$ids, prewhiten = TRUE)
pearsonStats <- rwi.stats(perfect, sim$ids, prewhiten = TRUE,
                          method = "pearson")
rbind(spearman = spearmanStats[, c("rbar.wt", "rbar.bt")],
      pearson = pearsonStats[, c("rbar.wt", "rbar.bt")])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
         rbar.wt rbar.bt
spearman   0.576   0.376
pearson    0.580   0.381
```


:::
:::




At seed 1 they are at 0.576 and 0.376 with `rwi.stats` as it comes, and at 0.580 and 0.381 with Pearson's correlation, against targets of 0.6 and 0.4. One collection is one draw, so here are twenty, built with seeds 1 to 20. Go straight to what was built, on the log scale with the true memory divided out (and with white climate, so there is only one memory to undo), and they average 0.600 and 0.400. So the collections are built to their targets. Two things take the numbers down from there.

The first is that `rwi.stats` works on indices and has to fit its own AR model. The parts are built on the log scale and the indices are their exponentials, and prewhitening fits an AR model to each core where the simulation knows the true one. With Pearson's correlation, the twenty collections average 0.586 and 0.389.

The second is the kind of correlation. `rwi.stats` uses Spearman's rank correlation unless you ask for another, and on normally distributed data Spearman's runs a little under Pearson's, by $(6/\pi)\arcsin(r/2)$ for a Pearson correlation $r$ [@Moran1948]. The targets are Pearson correlations, and a Pearson correlation of 0.6 or 0.4 comes out at about 0.582 or 0.385 as Spearman's. With the default, the twenty collections average 0.570 and 0.377.

So `rwi.stats` reports a few hundredths under the targets before any method has touched the rings, with each of the two steps taking about half. Keep that in mind when you compare a statistic from the simulation with the value it was built with.

## The Default Collection

[The Simulated Collection](03SimulatedCollection.qmd) has the table of what is planted in the collection built with `seed = 1`, tree by tree: which trees are crowded, which the event hits, the release and the missing ring.

## What Comes Back {#sec-sim-returns}

| Field | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `rwl` | The widths as measured, with any dating errors, from the first measured ring. Class `rwl`. |
| `ids` | The tree and core number of each series. |
| `truth$rwl` | The widths as the trees grew them, before any dating errors, from the oldest pith. Class `rwl`. |
| `truth$age` | $A_{it}$ for each core in mm, competition included. |
| `truth$memory.noise` | $M_{ijt}$ for each core: climate and noise after the tree's memory, on the log scale. |
| `truth$disturbance` | $D1_{it} + D2_{it}$ for each core, on the log scale. |
| `truth$climate` | A data frame of year and $C_t$, the climate as it went into the trees, on the log scale. |
| `truth$release` | The release as given: tree, year, size and decay. |
| `truth$event` | The event as given, plus `trees`, the numbers of the trees it hit. |
| `truth$errors` | The dating errors as given. |
| `truth$pith` | Each tree's name, pith year and outer ring. The outer ring is `end.year` for a living tree. |
| `truth$competition` | The names of the crowded trees. |
| `truth$sensitivity` | Each tree's multiplier on the climate. All 1 unless `sens.sdlog` is set. |
| `truth$growth` | Each tree's basal area increment and its trend with age, $\beta_i$. The trends are all 0 unless `bai.trend` is set. |
| `truth$params` | The other arguments, as used, including the seed. |

The parts multiply back into the widths. `truth$age * exp(truth$memory.noise + truth$disturbance)`, rounded to 0.01 mm, is `truth$rwl`.

## Arguments

| Argument | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `n.tree` | `20` | Number of trees. |
| `n.core` | `2` | Cores per tree, up to 26. |
| `end.year` | `2025` | The year the collection is cored, and the outside ring of every living tree. Dead trees end earlier (see `dead`). |
| `age.range` | `c(120, 380)` | Ages of the youngest and oldest trees. |
| `rbar.bt` | `0.4` | Target correlation between trees, the climate's share of $M_{ijt}$. |
| `rbar.wt` | `0.6` | Target correlation between cores of one tree, the share of climate and tree noise. |
| `sd.hf` | `0.25` | Standard deviation of $M_{ijt}$ on the log scale. |
| `phi` | `0.5` | The tree's memory, the AR(1) coefficient on climate and noise. |
| `climate` | `NULL` | A climate series named by year. `NULL` draws one. |
| `climate.phi` | `0.3` | Memory in the drawn climate. Ignored when you pass `climate`. |
| `sens.sdlog` | `0` | How much the trees' sensitivity to climate varies. `0` gives every tree the same. |
| `bai` | `600` | Basal area added each year by a typical tree, in mm². |
| `bai.sdlog` | `0.4` | How much growth rates vary from tree to tree. |
| `juv` | `25` | How quickly a young tree ramps up to its growth rate, in years. |
| `bai.age` | `0` | Correlation between a tree's log growth rate and its age. Negative values make old trees slow. |
| `bai.trend` | `0` | How much the trees' basal area increment changes with age, per century on the log scale. `0` gives every tree the same shape. |
| `compete` | `0.3` | Size of the competition wander on the log scale. `0` turns it off. |
| `compete.frac` | `0.5` | Share of the trees that are crowded. |
| `compete.phi` | `0.97` | How slowly the competition wander moves. |
| `pith.miss` | `5` | Mean number of rings by which a core misses the pith. |
| `dead` | `NULL` | Dead trees. `frac` is the share of trees that died and `span` how many years before `end.year` they could have died. `NULL` keeps every tree alive. |
| `release` | `list(tree = 10, year = 1950, size = log(2), decay = 25)` | $D1_{it}$ in one tree. `NULL` turns it off. |
| `event` | `list(year = 1880, frac = 0.5, size = -log(2), decay = 8)` | $D2_{it}$ in some of the trees. `NULL` turns it off. |
| `errors` | `data.frame(series = "SIM03A", year = 1800, type = "missing")` | Dating errors to plant. `NULL` plants none. |
| `site` | `"SIM"` | The site code at the start of each series name. |
| `digits` | `2` | Decimal places the widths are rounded to. |
| `seed` | `NULL` | A random seed. `NULL` gives a different collection every time. |

## Making Your Own

Change the arguments and you get a different collection. A few that the book uses:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# A clean collection: no release, no event and no dating errors
clean <- sim.collection(seed = 1, release = NULL, event = NULL, errors = NULL)

# A weak collection, where the trees agree about half as well
weak <- sim.collection(seed = 1, rbar.bt = 0.2, rbar.wt = 0.4)

# Open-grown trees only, under climate with no memory
open <- sim.collection(seed = 1, compete = 0, climate.phi = 0)

# Two missing rings in one core and a false ring in another
errs <- data.frame(series = c("SIM03A", "SIM03A", "SIM07B"),
                   year = c(1800, 1900, 1850),
                   type = c("missing", "missing", "false"))
messy <- sim.collection(seed = 1, errors = errs)
```
:::


The seed fixes every random draw, so the same call gives the same collection every time. Arguments that only set a size, like `rbar.bt`, `sd.hf`, `compete` or `climate.phi`, scale the same draws, so `weak` is the default collection with its agreement turned down. Arguments that change what gets drawn shift every draw after them. `sens.sdlog` above zero is one of those, so a collection with varied sensitivity has different noise and crowded trees from the default collection with the same seed. `dead` changes the years the collection covers, so it changes every draw after it, the climate included. `bai.age` uses the same draw for the growth rates and moves nothing else. `bai.trend` is drawn after everything else, so turning it on changes the age trends and leaves the climate, the noise and the crowded trees as they were. Turning the event off keeps the climate and the noise but picks different crowded trees, and passing your own climate gives you different trees altogether.

## What It Leaves Out

[The Simulated Collection](03SimulatedCollection.qmd) sets the collection beside Hurricane Ridge and lists what a collection from a site has that the simulation doesn't. A few of the simplifications favor particular methods, so keep them in mind when a method does better here than you expected.

- Every open-grown tree has the same shape of age trend, scaled by its growth rate, unless you set `bai.trend`. That suits a regional curve unusually well.
- The stem doesn't grow with its rings. The age trend comes from the area a tree adds each year, and climate, noise and disturbance then widen or narrow each ring. Those changes never feed back into the size of the stem, so a run of good years or a release doesn't spread later wood more thinly. By the bark, the radius the rings add up to differs from the one the age trend assumes by a few percent. Over 50 default collections the median core was 2.6% larger, and 98% of cores fell between 6% smaller and 15% larger. The release in tree 10 leaves its radius 6 to 7% larger by `end.year`.
- A tree's growth rate has nothing to do with its age unless you set `bai.age`. In the field, trees that grow slowly tend to live longer, and that biases a regional curve. [Regional Curves](12RegionalCurves.qmd) adds a link of its own to show what it does.
- Every tree is cored in the same year unless you set `dead`, so by default the collection has only living trees. [Regional Curves](12RegionalCurves.qmd) joins collections that end in different centuries to get past that.
- The simulated trees are all there is. There is no stand around them to choose them from, so the simulation can't show what picking trees by age, size or looks does to a collection.
- Rings go missing only where you plant the errors. A narrow ring always forms all the way around.
- The only measurement error is the rounding.
- There is one climate, felt with the same strength in every tree unless you set `sens.sdlog`, with no swing slower than its own memory unless you pass one in.
